title: Hosted Chat Quickstart + Console & Cost Controls Demo
summary: Intro demo of Redwood hosted chat generative API with console tour and cost controls. Focus on streaming behavior, key parameters (temperature, max_tokens, stop sequences), retry/backoff patterns, concurrency limits, and cost-saving levers (batching, caching, quantization recommendations). Customer raised HIPAA/data residency concerns and wanted examples for SSO, audit logs, and private deployment tradeoffs.
topics: Console: per-route cost and latency dashboards
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-07-29
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Ava Chen (Redwood AE), Marcus Bell (Redwood SE), Noah Ruiz (Redwood SE), Samantha Ortiz (BlueLeaf), Dev Patel (BlueLeaf), Lena Park (BlueLeaf), Tom Reyes (BlueLeaf)

Auto-summary (generated): Quickstart demo of hosted chat. Showed streaming behavior, plausible retry paths, console cost breakdown. Next steps: share playbook, run small pilot, security questionnaire.

--- Transcript (timestamps approx, transcription quality: medium) ---
[00:00] Ava (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Ava with Redwood Inference. Quick intros — Marcus is our SE and Noah is on the solutions side. How's everyone doing?
[00:07] Samantha (BlueLeaf): Good, thanks. We're excited — we've been evaluating a couple of options for adding conversational triage to patient support.
[00:14] Dev (BlueLeaf): Hi all. Technical crew on our side, I'm Dev, I manage infra.
[00:18] Lena (BlueLeaf): Lena — security. I'll be focused on compliance questions.
[00:22] Tom (BlueLeaf): Tom, product.
[00:25] Marcus (Redwood): Great, we'll jump into a hosted demo, show chat streaming, parameter choices, and then the console to surface latency and token cost. We'll also call out where dedicated or private deployments come in for security. Sound good?
[00:33] Samantha: Yep. Our main concerns are latency for real-time chat, cost at scale, and HIPAA considerations.
[00:40] Ava: Perfect, we'll tailor the demo. Marcus — want to kick off with streaming?
[00:44] Marcus: Sure. So first a quick high-level — the hosted API supports streaming responses over HTTP/2 and websockets, with chunked token events. I'm going to demo a simple chat call.
[00:55] [01:00] Marcus: (screen) Here's a sample request: model: "redwood-1-large" prompt: system + conversation, temperature 0.2, max_tokens 150, stream:true. Notice we can set partial responses streaming as they are generated — this reduces perceived latency.
[01:15] Dev: When you say perceived latency, how different is that from tail latency? If we have 100ms per token but long stalls, it affects UX.
[01:23] Marcus: Good point. Streaming helps because the client can render partial tokens immediately. Tail latency still matters; we optimize kernels, but we also recommend small max_new_tokens for chat turn starts. For heavier contexts we use prefix KV caching so the model doesn't recompute the whole history.
[01:40] Lena: Quick question, is the KV cache stored in customer VPC for private deploys?
[01:45] Noah (Redwood): For hosted, KV cache is ephemeral and encrypted; for Redwood Private in a VPC/on-prem the cache can be customer-managed and never leaves their network. We can walk through that in the security docs.
[01:57] Samantha: Ok good. Can you show a retry pattern — like if we hit a 5xx?
[02:01] Marcus: Yeah. Typical pattern: exponential backoff with jitter, and idempotency keys for non-streaming calls. For streaming we recommend layered retry: small-range reconnects to pick up remaining tokens when possible, and fallback to a sync generation if stream fails. Here's a code snippet for backoff (0.5s, 1s, 2s...).
[02:22] Tom: If we do reconnect, do we risk duplication of tokens?
[02:26] Marcus: Slight risk — we attach a sequence id and clients can dedupe. For chat we also recommend storing conversation state server-side with message checksums.
[02:36] [05:00] Marcus: Switching to parameters — temperature controls randomness; top_p is nucleus sampling; lower temperature + low top_p gives stable outputs for triage flows. For copy/summary we suggest temperature 0 - 0.3, for creative content 0.7+.
[05:20] Dev: Any cost impact from temperature?
[05:22] Ava: Not directly — cost is mostly tokens and model size. However, higher temperature can lead to longer outputs so indirectly more tokens.
[05:31] Marcus: Also max_tokens bounds output length. Use stop sequences to end early when you control turn boundaries.
[05:38] Samantha: We have strict redaction rules for PHI, are there built-in prompt patterns or tools?
[05:44] Noah: We recommend a pre-processing step that strips PHI at the client and a post-processing redaction layer. Redwood also supports data retention controls and can be configured to not store conversation contents in hosted mode for enterprise tiers; for full control you can go private.
[06:00] Lena: Do you have SOC2 reports and KMS options?
[06:03] Ava: Yes, SOC2 Type II available; we support customer-managed KMS for Private and dedicated, and we have HSM integration as an enterprise add-on. We'll send the security pack after the call.
[06:12] [08:30] Marcus: Now the console — here's per-route metrics: token usage, avg latency p50/p95, error rates. You can set per-route quotas and per-client API keys. One thing customers like is the token-level cost breakdown so product teams can see which flows are expensive.
[08:52] Tom: Can we see per-customer or per-team cost?
[08:55] Ava: Yes, billing can be split by API key tags; Dedicated customers often use this to allocate cost. In the console you can export CSVs for finance.
[09:05] Dev: How about batching and caching recommendations?
[09:08] Marcus: Under the Optimize tab we surface recommended batching windows and quantization levels depending on model architecture and sequences. For high throughput, batch size 8-32 depending on latency SLO and GPU. Also automatic prefix caching for repeated conversation starts. Note: our recommendations are workload-driven — we run sample traces and suggest an optimal config.
[09:28] Samantha: When you say quantization, do you mean int8/4-bit? How do quality regressions appear?
[09:34] Marcus: Right — int8 and mixed 4-bit paths. We also provide canary testing and evals against your prompt set so you can compare outputs before rolling out. Confidence thresholds and regression alerts tie into the console.
[09:48] [12:00] Marcus: Quick demo of a live chat stream — sending a patient triage prompt. (typing) The stream yields tokens every ~60ms in this sandbox. You see partial token groups, then finalization event. If I artificially kill the stream, client reconnect logic will try a small resume.
[12:20] Dev: That sandbox looked low-latency — what's typical for p95 in hosted?
[12:25] Ava: Depends on model and region. For redwood-1-medium we often see ~200-400ms p95 for short responses; larger models / longer contexts increase that. We publish benchmarks in the model catalog.
[12:38] Samantha: If we need sub-200ms consistently for a mobile app, is Dedicated the right fit?
[12:44] Marcus: Likely yes — Dedicated gives pinned GPU pools, and you can reserve capacity. There's tradeoff: higher fixed cost but lower variability. For some customers, a hybrid policy routes critical traffic to Dedicated and low-priority to Hosted.
[12:59] [15:00] Lena: If we go dedicated or private, what's the onboarding time?
[15:03] Noah: Dedicated setup: 2-4 weeks typical depending on capacity and region; Private (VPC) can be 4-8 weeks with network setup, KMS, and SOC compliance mapping. We have a runbook to accelerate it.
[15:17] Samantha: Is there a sandbox that mimics our data residency?
[15:20] Ava: We can spin up region-specific hosted endpoints in EU or US; for full residency guarantee, Private on-prem or VPC is the path.
[15:27] [18:00] Marcus: Back to retries — here's an example of idempotency: if you split user messages into atomic message IDs you can safely replay a generation request. For streaming, we include partial offsets so client can resume without duplicating earlier tokens.
[18:15] Dev: How do you recommend storing conversation state? Server-side or client?
[18:19] Marcus: Server-side is preferred for reproducibility and audit logs; client side is possible for lightweight UIs but server-side storage enables replay and dedupe.
[18:28] Samantha: Any pitfalls with caching and privacy?
[18:31] Noah: Yes — caching can store embeddings or prefixes. For PHI, you must ensure cache encryption and retention TTLs are aligned with policy. For hosted enterprise tiers we can disable certain caching or route to Private.
[18:45] [21:00] Tom: Walk me through a failure scenario — rate limit spike and fallback to smaller model?
[21:07] Marcus: We support smart routing policies: in high load we can automatically fallback to lower-cost compatible model variants; the console shows fallback counts. Also you can configure canary rules for A/B.
[21:20] Dev: How seamless is architecture change for the app? Does it need client changes to handle fallbacks?
[21:25] Marcus: Minimal — if you follow our SDK, fallbacks are transparent. But you should surface model metadata to UX so product can adjust messaging.
[21:33] [24:00] Marcus: Now a quick tour of the Optimize suggestions — it will recommend batch window size, KV cache TTL, quantization profile, and whether to pin a model to Dedicated. Each suggestion includes an estimated cost delta and latency impact.
[24:18] Samantha: Can we run a pilot with 10k monthly active users?
[24:22] Ava: Yes — we can create a pilot plan. We'll need expected RPS, average turn length, and allowed latency to properly size.
[24:30] Dev: We have about 8 RPS peak and average 120 tokens per turn currently.
[24:35] Marcus: Great, we can draft cost estimates in the next step.
[24:40] [27:00] Lena: On auditing — does Redwood provide per-token audit logs with redaction markers?
[27:05] Noah: We provide per-request logs including metadata. For content logging you can opt-in or disable storage. We can also provide a filtered audit trail that stores hashes instead of text.
[27:18] Samantha: That would be useful.
[27:20] Tom: Competitors we've looked at: Anthropic and OpenAI, their managed endpoints, and a self-hosted stack.
[27:27] Ava: Understood — we'll include a comparison doc.
[27:32] [30:00] Marcus: Quick Q&A: Dev asked about SDK retry helpers — our SDK includes built-in retry/backoff helpers and reconnect helpers for websockets. Use idempotency keys for non-streaming generation.
[30:14] Dev: Are there per-request cost controls in the API?
[30:18] Marcus: You can set max_tokens, stop sequences, and per-route quotas; in the console you can set hard limits per API key. Also token inflation monitoring warns on unexpectedly large prompts.
[30:30] Samantha: For prompts that contain PHI, what do you recommend for encryption at rest?
[30:34] Noah: Use customer-managed KMS and ensure you enable data-at-rest encryption. We'll provide config examples in the security pack.
[30:44] [33:00] Marcus: Demo wrap-up — showed streaming, parameter controls, retries, console and optimize recommendations.
[33:10] Tom: That was helpful. One more thing — how can we measure quality regressions when quantizing?
[33:15] Marcus: We run prompt-set A/B evals and provide regression alerts. You can upload your test prompts and we'll run them across candidate quantized models and report metrics.
[33:30] [36:00] Ava: Let's recap next steps and owners.
[36:05] Ava: We'll send security pack and SOC2 docs (Ava). Marcus will run a quick pilot sizing and cost estimate from Dev's RPS and token numbers. Noah will prepare notes on caching options and private deploy timeline.
[36:25] Samantha: Can we get a hands-on sandbox with our prompts?
[36:28] Marcus: Yes — we can provision a sandbox tenant.
[36:31] Dev: Timeline — we'd like a pilot in the next 4 weeks.
[36:34] Ava: We'll aim for that.
[36:36] [40:00] (Some cross-talk about calendar invites and who to include)
[40:12] Lena: I'll need the security questionnaire filled out and a point of contact for our compliance team.
[40:18] Ava: We'll assign a CSM and SE for onboarding.
[40:22] Tom: Any documents to share now?
[40:25] Ava: Yes — security pack, model catalog benchmarks, and a pilot cost template. We'll send after the call.
[40:33] [45:00] Marcus: Final quick note — for lower cost we often suggest two levers: batching for throughput flows and automatic prefix caching for repeated prompts. Both can reduce token spend and GPU time by 20-50% depending on workload.
[45:20] Samantha: Great. Thanks everyone.
[45:25] Ava: Thanks all, we'll follow up with the items discussed.
[45:30] End of recording.
